segments.text: I wanted to see if I could improve this SHA-3 implementation.
Here's what I tried and what I found.
Start with Oxides Quartz Core. One byte arrives each clock. Two block buffers let
it fill the next block while processing the previous one. That's a good match for
its byte stream workload. With the full-rate adapter this integration
reaches nearly a hundred megabytes per second.

chapters.title: Compact: absorb directly into the state

segments.text: Now look at the wider path. DMA already delivers 8 bytes at a time. I feed those through a small buffer straight into the hash state.
Both full block buffers disappear. The digest reads the state itself. Capture and absorption still takes separate cycles, and the permutation still takes 24 rounds.
The next step was simplifying the surrounding logic.
Padding only touches 17 lanes so the selector doesn't need to reach across all 25.
I also register framing errors before updating the state.
The compact version keeps the same simulated cycle count, with fewer stand-alone lookup tables.
Now, look at the resource counts. About 23% fewer lookup tables, 58% fewer flip-flops.
Those totals include the local adapters, so we're comparing the complete routed hash partitions.
Both use zero block RAM and zero DSP blocks.
Both cores use the same board, shell, driver, and 100 megahertz clock.
I compare the median of seven samples after warm-up, checking every digest against software.
